content: Good afternoon. So today I want to walk you through something I have been thinking about seriously for the last several weeks. It has been brewing since the spring, honestly, but I finally have enough concrete information to bring it to you properly. We have been using the rear of the restaurant as basically a catch-all for dry goods, extra equipment, folded linen stock, and things we do not use every service but cannot quite justify getting rid of. It works in the sense that the stuff has somewhere to live, but when I stand back there and actually look at it, I see about twenty square meters of prime real estate in Higashi-Azabu being used to store canned tomatoes and spare tablecloths. And the more I think about the positioning we want to build toward over the next two years, the more that starts to feel like a genuine missed opportunity. I have been in conversation with Yamamoto Koumuten about converting it, and I now have an estimate in hand. I wanted to think through the full business case with you before I commit to anything.

This sounds like a significant capital decision, and the kind of thing that deserves careful analysis rather than a quick reaction to the headline number. Let me make sure I understand the concept before we get into the financials. When you say the storage area at the rear, how large is the footprint we are actually talking about, and what is the conversion concept? Are you looking at additional main dining capacity, a private event space, a bar or lounge extension, or something else entirely? And what does the Yamamoto Koumuten estimate cover in terms of scope and cost? I want the full picture before we start modeling anything.

Right, let me walk you through the specifics. The plan is to convert storage area at rear into an 8-seat private room. That is the core of it. The space is roughly twelve tatami equivalent in floor area, which works out to about twenty square meters once you account for the irregular shape of the back wall. There is a column intrusion on the left side that cuts into the usable floor area slightly, but the room planner from Yamamoto Koumuten has already accounted for that in the layout. The concept is a fully enclosed room with its own dedicated entrance from the main dining room, so guests using the private room do not need to walk through or past other tables in either direction. Soundproofed properly, not symbolically, meaning a table having a sensitive business conversation does not have to worry about being overheard by the main dining room. And finished to exactly the same standard as the rest of the restaurant: custom joinery, proper architectural lighting designed for the mood of dinner service, the same tableware and linen program we use in the main room. Not a curtained-off corner with a folding table and different energy, but a room that feels like it genuinely belongs to the same restaurant. That distinction matters for the pricing rationale I will get to in a moment. On the cost side: Yamamoto Koumuten, which is Tetsuo Yamamoto's firm, the same crew that built the original space three years ago, came back with an estimate of 1.4 million yen for the full conversion. That covers the partition wall construction, the acoustic treatment and soundproofing layer, a dedicated HVAC branch so the room has independent climate control from the main dining room, a complete lighting redesign, and all finish work including the joinery. Tetsuo walked the space thoroughly and I trust the estimate is solid. His crew built the place originally so there will be no structural surprises.

1.4 million yen for a properly executed private room of that specification is within the realistic range I would expect for quality restaurant fit-out in central Tokyo. The breakdown you have described, partition wall, acoustic treatment, independent HVAC, dedicated lighting design, and full finish work, is what a genuine private dining room actually requires to function as you are describing. Soundproofing and independent HVAC in particular are not optional luxuries if you want guests to feel genuinely private, and those two line items alone account for a substantial portion of that budget. The fact that Yamamoto Koumuten built the original space is a real advantage: they understand what is behind the walls, they will not encounter structural surprises mid-project, and their estimate is considerably more reliable than a cold bid from a contractor who has never seen the building. Before we get into the return on investment modeling, I want to raise the question that tends to get underweighted in this type of conversion decision. You are calling it a storage area, but storage areas in restaurant operations are functional infrastructure, not wasted space. Where does that dry goods inventory, that equipment, those linen stocks actually go once the room is built? If you are displacing meaningful operational storage without a clear solution, the conversion creates a problem somewhere else in the building that will cost you something to resolve, either in logistics friction, in renting external space, or in a combination of both. Have you worked through the storage relocation piece?

That is exactly the question I have been wrestling with, and I want to be honest that it took me longer than it should have to actually go solve it rather than just assume it would work out. What I found is that there is a building about two minutes walk from here, diagonally behind us on the far side of the block, that has small basement units available for commercial storage tenants. The landlord is a property management company rather than an individual, so the lease terms are straightforward and there is no ambiguity about the arrangement. I have already walked the specific unit that would work for us: it is below grade with no natural light obviously, but it is clean, it is dry, the access corridor is wide enough to bring in larger items, and the distance from the restaurant is genuinely walkable. Petrelli or one of the prep team could make the run during morning prep without it adding more than ten minutes to the workflow in either direction. The landlord is asking 38,000 yen monthly for the basement rental nearby. So the storage problem is solvable, but it is not free, and I want to be completely clear-eyed about that cost being part of the overall picture rather than treating the 1.4 million yen as the total outlay.

I am glad you have already walked a specific unit rather than assuming something would be available. That is the right due diligence on what could otherwise become a post-commitment operational headache. 38,000 yen monthly is a real number and it deserves to be treated as a perpetual ongoing cost rather than a minor rounding line item. Annualized, that is 456,000 yen per year running indefinitely as long as you are operating the private room. Most people who evaluate this kind of conversion frame it as a one-time capital decision against a single headline number. But the storage displacement creates a permanent structural cost that changes the full picture considerably. The true financial architecture here is: 1.4 million yen upfront in construction, plus 456,000 yen per year in perpetual basement rental that begins the moment you start build and never stops, plus whatever amortization charge you assign to the construction cost itself. The private room does not just need to generate incremental revenue above your current baseline. It needs to generate enough incremental revenue to clear that ongoing baseline cost before any real return on the capital begins to accumulate. I want to build that math out properly once I understand the revenue model. But first, what is the concept for the room itself, what are you planning to call it, and what is the pricing structure you have in mind?

The revenue model is where I think the business case gets genuinely compelling, and this is the part I have spent the most time thinking through. The room would be called Sala Modena. I have had that name in mind for quite a while. It references the province in Emilia-Romagna where Petrelli grew up, and it gives the space a specific identity that is rooted in the same culinary story the restaurant already tells. That framing matters because I do not want to market it as the private room at Osteria Morishita, which sounds like a functional afterthought rather than a destination. Sala Modena is something guests request by name and associate with a particular kind of experience. The pricing model is built around a room minimum spend rather than a per-head cover charge, structured so that the minimum for the room overall is meaningfully higher than what eight guests at the standard tasting menu rate would spend in the main dining room. The premium pricing is intentional and justified on several grounds: the exclusivity of having the space entirely to yourselves, the absolute privacy, the dedicated single-table service attention throughout the meal, and the celebratory or business entertainment context in which private dining typically occurs. Private dining groups also tend to spend significantly more on wine than main dining room tables at comparable per-head spend, because they are not self-conscious about lingering or ordering another bottle when there is no ambient pressure from surrounding guests. My projection based on what I have observed at comparable establishments is that per-head spend in Sala Modena will run 25 to 35 percent above the main dining room average. I have run rough numbers on a two-evening-per-week baseline at full capacity, and the incremental revenue figure is substantial enough that the investment looks genuinely attractive.

The name Sala Modena is a strong creative decision. It is specific enough to carry genuine authenticity, it connects directly to Petrelli's background and the culinary identity of the restaurant, and it signals that the space has a story and a provenance rather than just a function. Guests who have done private dining in Tokyo hotel ballrooms or at larger restaurant groups will feel the difference between booking a generic private room and booking Sala Modena, and that distinction is exactly what allows premium pricing to hold without feeling arbitrary or extractive. The 25 to 35 percent per-head premium over your main dining room average is plausible and consistent with private dining economics I have seen at restaurants operating at a comparable positioning level. But I want to stress-test the utilization assumption carefully, because that is where projections in this category consistently run optimistic. Two evenings per week at full capacity means 96 private dining covers per month through that room alone. That is a healthy booking rhythm, but it is not the rhythm a room achieves in its first month of existence. Private dining volume builds through channels that take real time to develop: corporate entertainment relationships cultivated one account at a time, event organizers who need to discover and vet a new space before they add it to their recommendation list, and repeat guests who return for anniversaries and milestones. In my experience, a new private dining room at a restaurant of your size and positioning takes six to twelve months before it reaches anything resembling a steady-state booking rate. So let us walk through the conservative scenario with care. If Sala Modena runs at one evening per week on average across the first six months, what does the monthly revenue figure actually look like, and how does it compare to the 38,000 yen monthly baseline cost plus the construction amortization?

The conservative scenario is tighter and I want to own that honestly. At one evening per week with eight covers running at the premium pricing I am planning, the monthly revenue from Sala Modena probably comes in somewhere between 280,000 and 340,000 yen, with the range driven primarily by wine spend variability. Corporate entertainment groups tend to be more generous on wine than family celebration dinners in my experience, so the composition of the booking mix matters quite a bit to where in that range you actually land. Against that revenue, if I subtract the 38,000 yen monthly for the basement rental and then amortize the 1.4 million yen construction cost over three years, which I think is the appropriate horizon for a capital decision at this scale and for this type of asset, the monthly amortization charge runs about 39,000 yen. So the combined direct costs attributable to Sala Modena are roughly 77,000 yen per month. On the conservative revenue estimate, that leaves somewhere between 200,000 and 260,000 yen per month in margin contribution, which is a real and positive number. But it assumes every booking is a full eight-cover party, and reality will have some six-person groups, some last-minute cancellations within the refund window, and some evenings where the booking simply does not materialize. You are right that the utilization assumption is the most load-bearing variable in the whole model. Where I believe the conservative case becomes substantially less conservative is if I can anchor at least one corporate account into a recurring booking pattern. I have had preliminary conversations with two or three clients in this neighborhood who entertain regularly and carry standing monthly budgets for business dinners. Each of them has told me unprompted that they wish there were a proper private dining option in Higashi-Azabu. The hotel private rooms are too formal and too expensive for most of what they actually need. The private rooms at the larger izakaya chains in the area do not have the culinary level they are looking for. Sala Modena fits precisely into that gap, and I think if I approach those conversations with the specific offer, I have a real chance of converting at least one of them into something durable.

The cost structure you have described is more favorable than I anticipated for the conservative scenario. At 77,000 yen per month in direct costs assigned to Sala Modena, a single well-attended private dinner most weeks already generates meaningful margin contribution before any other bookings or upside materializes. That tells me the premium pricing architecture is doing real structural work in the economics, and that the room is not dependent on an aggressive or optimistic utilization rate just to cover its ongoing costs. That is an important sign. The corporate anchor account point is the most strategically important variable in this entire decision, and I want to spend a moment on what it actually means for your risk profile. What you have described, two or three clients in the immediate area who entertain at sufficient frequency and spend level to fill Sala Modena on a recurring basis, and who have independently and unprompted named this exact gap in the local market, is a materially different situation from speculating that corporate demand will show up after the room is built. The difference between those two scenarios is the difference between a demand signal you have heard directly and a demand assumption you are making. Virtually everything in your year-one projection depends on which category you are actually in. My strong recommendation before you finalize any commitment to Yamamoto Koumuten is to have a substantive conversation with at least one of those contacts specifically about Sala Modena. Not a vague mention that you are thinking about building something private. A real conversation with specifics: eight seats, fully enclosed, premium pricing, this is the culinary experience we are offering in this room, does this solve a recurring problem for you on a monthly or bi-monthly basis? You do not need a signed contract or a deposit check. You need a clear enough signal to distinguish genuine recurring interest from polite enthusiasm. That signal should come before construction starts, not after the room exists and you are working backward to fill it. Now walk me through the timing in full detail, because the scheduling of this build is the third dimension I need to understand before we can form a complete picture.

The timing is actually one of the primary reasons I am treating this as time-sensitive right now rather than deferring it until fall or winter. Tetsuo Yamamoto has availability in his construction schedule that aligns almost perfectly with our seasonal calendar, and the window he has offered me is specific. The construction window is 4 weeks, July 14 to August 9. That is the period he needs to complete the full scope: structural partition framing, acoustic treatment, HVAC branch routing, and all finish work. He is confident in that four-week estimate because, again, his crew built the original space and they know exactly what they are working with behind the walls. There will be no exploratory demolition and no guessing about load paths or hidden service routes. The reason the July 14 to August 9 window appeals to me so strongly is our seasonal traffic pattern. Our main dining room historically drops significantly through the summer, particularly around the Bon holiday period when a large portion of our regular clientele leaves Tokyo for travel or returns to their home regions. We lose a meaningful share of our corporate entertainment traffic because the people who make booking decisions are on summer leave, and the ambient dining-out rate in this part of Higashi-Azabu falls noticeably. Last August we were running at roughly 60 to 65 percent of our spring capacity for about three weeks. If construction at the rear of the building is going to create any operational disruption, it is far less costly to absorb that during a period when we are already at 60 percent than it would be in October or November when we are building momentum toward the year-end corporate calendar. Yamamoto Koumuten has also mapped out the construction phases for me in some detail. The most intrusive work, the structural partition framing and the HVAC penetration and routing, happens in the first eight to ten days of the window. After that it transitions to finish carpentry, acoustic lining installation, and the electrical work for the new lighting system, none of which generates the same level of noise or crew foot traffic through the building. And if the build completes on schedule by August 9, that gives us the remainder of August to fit out the room and soft-launch Sala Modena before September, when our traffic picks back up and the fall corporate entertainment season begins.

The July 14 to August 9 window is well-reasoned, and the seasonal logic behind your timing holds up. You are deliberately absorbing the highest-disruption phase of construction during the period when that disruption costs the least in foregone revenue, and you are targeting completion with enough runway before September to do a genuine soft launch rather than opening Sala Modena under time pressure with unresolved build snags. That sequencing reflects genuine operational discipline, not just convenient calendar scheduling. A few additions to the timing picture before you treat it as finalized. First, the phrase remainder of August to soft-launch Sala Modena is only realistic if the design and procurement decisions for the room are made before construction starts, not after. The pattern I have seen go wrong: construction finishes on August 9, and then you spend the first two or three weeks of August selecting chairs, chasing furniture delivery lead times, resolving lighting snags with the electrician, and writing the service protocol for the room from scratch. Your soft launch then becomes mid-September rather than late August, and you have lost the entire runway you thought you had before the fall season. I would treat all interior decisions, seating configuration, table and linen specification, the lighting program for dinner service, the exact tableware plan for Sala Modena, and the service protocol as work that must be completed in June and early July, running in parallel with the construction commitment, not sequentially after the room is physically done. Second, on the corporate account conversations: you have from today until July 14, roughly five weeks, to have those conversations properly. That is enough time to meet substantively with all three of the contacts you mentioned, not just one. I would use that window intentionally. Third, let me place the complete financial picture in one place now that we have all the numbers. You are committing to 1.4 million yen in upfront construction cost. You are taking on 38,000 yen monthly for the basement rental nearby as a perpetual operating line that begins as soon as construction starts. You are accepting some degree of main dining room disruption during the 4 weeks, July 14 to August 9 build window, in a period when attendance is already running soft. Against all of that, you have a room built to a standard that justifies premium pricing, operating under the Sala Modena identity which is a well-conceived brand decision, in a local market where multiple qualified prospective customers have independently named the precise gap you are filling. The conservative scenario at one evening per week generates positive margin contribution from the first month of operation. Any anchor corporate account changes the return profile substantially. And the build timing is structured to minimize the revenue cost of disruption while positioning you for a September launch into a recovering traffic period. My overall assessment is that this is a sound investment with a risk profile you can manage, provided the pre-launch work is executed with real discipline. Lock in the basement storage arrangement before breaking ground. Finalize Sala Modena's interior design by the end of June, not after August 9. Have all three corporate account conversations this month and next. And hold Yamamoto Koumuten to the 4 weeks, July 14 to August 9 schedule without slippage, because any overrun eats directly into the runway you need before September. If those conditions are in place when construction begins, I think you are in a well-structured position to move forward.
